notes: The primary control is the existing immediate opener in the same final source revision, using the same relaxed fake-indexeddb adapter, matching SQL and transaction boundaries. The new controller is opt-in; existing default APIs and raw SQLM/PGMM snapshot encodings are retained.

100,000-row measurements run separately after the repository validation and before browser tests/profiling: three warmups, nine samples. Optional 1,000,000-row checks use three warmups and five samples. Setup, initial checkpoint/index construction, final all-row validation, recovery and cleanup are outside timing. The reopen workload measures opening, a point read, and close explicitly.

Sparse/batch/coalesced saves include storage acknowledgement. The separately labelled enqueue workload deliberately excludes persistence. Codec-to-backend captureAndQueueMsPerBatch is a wall-time diagnostic mean across warmup and measured iterations, not a CPU clock or component of the median.

Ordinary measured sparse saves have zero full snapshot encodes and serialize only changed rows (SQLite once, PostgreSQL across three codec passes); at most 64 KiB submitted page bytes. Checkpoints, schema changes, opaque mutations and configured compaction still require full serialization and are outside the steady-delta timing claim.

Real WebKit uses the published browser bundles and actual IndexedDB/localStorage adapters. The added buffered test updates indexed keys through 100 individual transactions, awaits one save, separately observes an autonomous one-second timer save BEFORE flush/close, and checks close/reopen plus page reload. It retains 100,000 rows and exact prior counters for both engines. Timers and page-hide are best effort; one writer per key, recent unsaved changes may be lost.

The 32x32 persistent-map layout is retained. Larger synthetic layouts reduce fork work but did not deliver at least 20% real SQL write improvement without repeatable read/scan regressions above 5%. Actual SQL experiments retain three alternating rounds, ten warmups and 31 samples per layout.

The retained pre-buffered local bundles already include the earlier uncommitted large-table optimization pass. They are not a clean checkout of baselineCommit; their hashes identify the exact diagnostic comparison. Final bundles use the same Bun build target. Current source and browser bundles include the final opt-in statement execution hooks.

Default-runtime diagnostics retain noisy mixed-process pairs (five warmups, 21 samples per build, three alternating rounds). These show small SQLite transaction slowdowns; universal improvement is not claimed. Fresh-process 100,000-row read/scan pairs (ten warmups, 31 samples, three alternating rounds) did not repeat a >5% read/scan regression, but one PostgreSQL read outlier remains in the raw data. No layout change is justified by the noisy results.

CPU profiles run after timings and include imports, setup, validation/recovery and periodic compaction. The immediate profile is dominated by packed-column encoding, row materialization and full-image page comparison; buffered profiling shifts toward fake-indexeddb key handling, iteration and cloning. Profile iteration counts are diagnostic and are not the steady-delta benchmark.

Initial focused checks caught missing additive API documentation; a mixed recovery history caught an empty-slab adoption issue and mutable comparison journals after rollback. Both are fixed with retained regression tests. The performance gate caught repeated temporary-array access during batch capture; access is now hoisted without weakening the work budget. Borrowed bytea inputs/results preserve the existing aliasing behavior through a conservative checkpoint fallback.

All existing SQL differential/fuzz, deterministic wire, native container and compatibility tests remain authoritative. These measurements do not establish generic WASM/OPFS parity, multi-writer server concurrency, or suitability for every production workload.
